|publisher=Geological Society of America |language=en |doi=10.1130/2022.1220(21) |isbn=978-0-8137-1220-8 |last2=Peters |first2=Shanan E. |editor2-last=Williams |editor2-first=Michael L. |editor3-last=Kellett |editor3-first=Dawn A. |editor4-last=Tikoff |editor4-first=Basil}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Riding |first1=James B. |last2=Worley |first2=Noel E. |date=2020-05-30 Negus Prize to graduate students of biology since 2019.<ref name=":02" />

== Early life and education ==
Negus was born Christina L. Batty in Grantham, [[Lincolnshire]], England.<ref name=":3">{{Cite web |last=Montoro |first=Juan Carlos Gil |date=2024-08-15 |title=La vida es compleja: Charnia masoni pudo haber sido Charnia battyae |trans-title=Life is complex: Charnia masoni may have been Charnia battyae |url=https://naukas.com/2024/08/15/la-vida-es-compleja-charnia-masoni-pudo-haber-sido-charnia-battyae/ |access-date=2024-09-20 |website=Naukas |language=es}}</ref> Growing up in "[[Lias Group|Liassic]] (limestone sediments of [[Early Jurassic]], about 200 to 180 million years old) sandstones and clays", as she described her upbringing, her childhood activities were mostly collecting fossils, and was familiar with [[ammonites]] and [[belemnite]]s.<ref name=":1" /> During her school vacations, she explored interesting geological sites such as [[Peak District]] and Kent. During her secondary schooling, she read a small handbook ''Geology of the Ancient Rocks of Charnwood Forest, Leicestershire'' (1947)<ref>{{Cite book |last=Watts |first=William Whitehead |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=8OoINAAACAAJ |title=Geology of the Ancient Rocks of Charnwood Forest, Leicestershire: With which is Included the Area about Mountsorrel; Parts of the One-inch Maps (new Series) 141, 155 and 156 |date=1947 |publisher=Leicester Literary and Philosophical Society |pages=1–160 |language=en}}</ref> by [[William Whitehead Watts]],<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Bennett |first1=F.W. |last2=Lowe |first2=E.E. |last3=Gregory |first3=H.H. |last4=Jones |first4=F. |date=1928 |title=The geology of Charnwood Forest |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0016787828800149 |journal=Proceedings of the Geologists' Association |language=en |volume=39 |issue=3 |pages=241–IN6 |doi=10.1016/S0016-7878(28)80014-9|bibcode=1928PrGA...39..241B |url-access=subscription }}</ref> who had documented the Precambrian (roughly older than 530 million years ago) nature of the Charnwood rocks.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Carney |first=John N. |date=1999 |title=Revisiting the Charnian Supergroup: new advances in understanding old rocks |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1046/j.1365-2451.1999.00006.x |journal=Geology Today |language=en |volume=15 |issue=6 |pages=221–229 |doi=10.1046/j.1365-2451.1999.00006.x |bibcode=1999GeolT..15..221C |issn=0266-6979|url-access=subscription }}</ref> This information inspired her for a field visit to Charnwood.<ref name=":1" />

Enthused by her passion for fossils, she applied for an A level course in geology but her headmistress would not allow it. She therefore took [[A-level (United Kingdom)|A levels]] in zoology, botany, geography and art. She continued with an undergraduate course in zoology, botany and geography at the University of Reading in 1961 and completed the degree with honours in zoology. She then continued with a postgraduate research-based MSc in ecology at the same university. After her master's degree, she briefly joined [[Durham University]].<ref name="Negus 1966 513–532" /> After her marriage, she gave up career in academics and developed her talents in painting, sculpting, photography and poetry.<ref name="Becky" />

== Discovery of the Precambrian fossil ==

=== First discovery ===
For the 1956 summer vacation, Negus persuaded her family to explore Charnwood Forest with of pretext of collecting [[blueberries]]. According to her memory, it would have been around June and July as the blueberries were not yet ripe. That was not her priority, but instead was searching for fossils among the deepest rocks exposed. Furnished with maps from Watts's book, she already knew the best locations to look for. At an abandoned quarry of [[turbidites]] (a type of [[sedimentary rocks]] deposited from [[turbidity currents]] of oceans), she found large slabs of rocks inclined to form a wall. The rock faces were too smooth and vertical that she could only scrape along the lower bases. Hidden behind some roots and thickets, she saw a clear impression on one rock that looked like a fern.<ref name=":3"/> She also knew that it was not a proper fern as the frond had no stem or branching veins.<ref name=":2" /> It was obvious to her that it was a fossil in a Precambrian rock. Her parents did not have connections with scientists so they only encouraged her to tell her teachers.<ref name=":3"/>

For Negus, the closest to a scientist in palaeontology was her geography teacher. As she described the discovery, her teacher was not interested and simply said that there were no fossils in Precambrian rocks, that what she found was either not a fossil or the rocks were much younger. She could not convince anyone, but her confidence remained unfeigned. During winter vacation of that year in December, she again asked her parents to make another trip to Charnwood Forest. Then equipped with her father's coal hammer, she tried to extract the fossils from the rock slab, but only to find that the hand-tool could not make a crack on the [[hard rock]].<ref name=":3"/> Instead, Negus took a pencil and made a stencil trace of the fossil on two sheets of paper. Trying to identify the fossil herself, she searched through all possible information from books and local museum, but found no matching image of her ancient frond. She kept her pencil rubbing in a folder for any future clue.<ref name=":2" />

=== Rediscovery and identification ===
In May 1957, [[Roger Mason (geologist)|Roger Mason]], Richard Blatchford and Richard Allen from [[Wyggeston Grammar School for Boys]] in Leicester went rock-climbing in the Charnwood Forest. It was Blachford who first spotted the fossil imprint and thought it was a feather. A 15-year-old Mason climbed down to the spot and found that it was more fern-like. He already knew that the rocks were of Precambrian origin and nobody expected fossils of that kind. He took a rubbing of it and showed it to his father at home. Mason's father was a teacher at the [[University of Leicester]] and quickly approached his young colleague and geologist, [[Trevor D. Ford]]. Sceptical of a fossil in Precambrian rocks, Ford and the Masons went to Charnwood Forest and confirmed the fossil.<ref name="Mason-2007-Disc">{{cite web |last=Mason |first=Roger |year=2007 |title=The discovery of Charnia masoni |url=http://www.le.ac.uk/gl/charnia2007/AbstractBooklet2007r.pdf |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210308141852/https://www.le.ac.uk/gl/charnia2007/AbstractBooklet2007r.pdf |archive-date=8 March 2021 |access-date=5 April 2016 |website=[[University of Leicester]]}}</ref>

In September 1957, Ford had professional miners excavate the rock and extract the fossil for display at the [[Leicester Museum & Art Gallery]] (New Walk Museum and Art Gallery, prior to 2022).<ref name=":3" /> Ford made further exploration of Charnwood Forest for any other specimens and found five more fern-like specimens and twelve ring-like fossils. Upon analysis, he identified the two types of fossils as algae, and for the fern-like type he created the scientific name ''[[Charnia masoni]]'', to credit the place and discoverer.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Bowers |first=A. |date=2013 |title=Precambrian fossil discoveries and new fossil localities in Charnwood Forest, Leicestershire |url= |journal=Mercian Geologist |volume=18 |pages=91−98 |s2cid=131624603}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Ford |first=Trevor D. |date=1980-01-01 |title=The Ediacaran fossils of Charnwood Forest, Leicestershire |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0016787880800149 |journal=Proceedings of the Geologists' Association |volume=91 |issue=1 |pages=81–83 |doi=10.1016/S0016-7878(80)80014-9 |bibcode=1980PrGA...91...81F |issn=0016-7878|url-access=subscription }}</ref> He reported the description in the September 1958 issue of the ''[[Proceedings of the Yorkshire Geological Society]]'', drawing a conclusion: <blockquote>Several specimens of two new fossils recently found in the Woodhouse Beds of the Charnwood Forest Pre-Cambrian succession are described and named ''Charnia masoni'' and ''[[Charniodiscus|Charniodiscus concentricus]].''.. The evidence points to their being algae.<ref name="Ford_1958">{{cite journal |author=Ford, T.D. |year=1958 |title=Precambrian fossils from Charnwood Forest |journal=Yorkshire Geological Society Proceedings |volume=31 |issue=3 |pages=211–217 |bibcode=1958PYGS...31..211F |doi=10.1144/pygs.31.3.211}}</ref> </blockquote>''Charnia masoni'' became the most iconic<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Dunn |first1=Frances S. |last2=Wilby |first2=Philip R. |last3=Kenchington |first3=Charlotte G. |last4=Grazhdankin |first4=Dmitriy V. |last5=Donoghue |first5=Philip C. J. |last6=Liu |first6=Alexander G. |date=2019 |title=Anatomy of the Ediacaran rangeomorph Charnia masoni |journal=Papers in Palaeontology |volume=5 |issue=1 |pages=157–176 |doi=10.1002/spp2.1234 |issn=2056-2802 |pmc=6472560 |pmid=31007942|bibcode=2019PPal....5..157D }}</ref> and first ever known Precambrian organism.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Antcliffe |first1=Jonathan B. |last2=Brasier |first2=Martin D. |date=2008 |title=Charnia at 50: Developmental models for Ediacaran fronds |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1475-4983.2007.00738.x |journal=Palaeontology |language=en |volume=51 |issue=1 |pages=11–26 |doi=10.1111/j.1475-4983.2007.00738.x |bibcode=2008Palgy..51...11A |issn=0031-0239|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Bowers |first=A. |date=2014 |title=Further Precambrian (Ediacaran) fossil discoveries in Charnwood Forest, Leicestershire |url=https://www.monash.edu/__data/assets/pdf_file/0009/85626/mercian-2014-v18-p175-further-ediacaran-fossils-charwood-forest-bowers.pdf |journal=Mercian Geologist |volume=18 |pages=175−179 |s2cid=55579161}}</ref>{{Efn|Other fossils later identified as belonging to Precambrian were discovered earlier, such as  ''Aspidella'' from Newfoundland in 1868 and ''Dickinsonia'' from the Ediacaran Hills, Australia, in 1947, but their nature as fossils and their geological age were not established until the 1960s.}}

=== Negus's pursuit ===
Not knowing that her fossil had been described and reported, Negus returned to Charnwood Forest in 1958, only to discover that the fossil had been extracted and disappeared. As soon as she entered the University of Reading in 1961, she took her fossil tracing to the geologist there for identification only to discover that her fossil had been described three years before. Her contribution to the fossil discovery was lost until 2004,<ref name="Becky" /> when she saw Mason, who was then a geologist at the [[University College London]],<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Mason |first1=Roger |last2=She |first2=Zhenbing |date=2022 |title=Will there be Unexpected Geological Discoveries? |url=https://link.springer.com/10.1007/s12583-022-1742-x |journal=Journal of Earth Science |language=en |volume=33 |issue=5 |pages=1337 |doi=10.1007/s12583-022-1742-x |bibcode=2022JEaSc..33.1337M |issn=1674-487X}}</ref> talking about the discovery of ''Charnia'' on a television programme.<ref name="Becky" /> By then, ''Charnia'' and other [[Ediacaran]] fossils became famous as evidence of Precambrian life,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Brasier |first1=Martin |last2=Antcliffe |first2=Jonathan |date=2004-08-20 |title=Paleobiology. Decoding the Ediacaran enigma |url=https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.1102673 |journal=Science |volume=305 |issue=5687 |pages=1115–1117 |doi=10.1126/science.1102673 |issn=1095-9203 |pmid=15326344|url-access=subscription }}</ref> which had remained one of the biggest puzzles in the history of life on Earth and the so called "Darwin's dilemma".<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Kutschera |first1=Ulrich |last2=Niklas |first2=KarlJ. |date=2004 |title=The modern theory of biological evolution: an expanded synthesis |url=http://link.springer.com/10.1007/s00114-004-0515-y |journal=Naturwissenschaften |language=en |volume=91 |issue=6 |pages=255–276 |doi=10.1007/s00114-004-0515-y |pmid=15241603 |bibcode=2004NW.....91..255K |issn=0028-1042|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Conway Morris |first=Simon |date=2006-06-29 |title=Darwin's dilemma: the realities of the Cambrian 'explosion' |journal=Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences |language=en |volume=361 |issue=1470 |pages=1069–1083 |doi=10.1098/rstb.2006.1846 |issn=0962-8436 |pmc=1578734 |pmid=16754615}}</ref> In introducing the theory of [[natural selection]] in 1859, Darwin argues that the absence of such ancient lives was "the most obvious and gravest objection" to his theory.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Darwin |first=Charles |url=https://darwin-online.org.uk/content/frameset?itemID=F373&viewtype=text&pageseq=1 |title=On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection |date=1859 |publisher=John Murray |location=London |page=280 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Burchfield |first=Joe D. |date=1974 |title=Darwin and the Dilemma of Geological Time |url=https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/10.1086/351300 |journal=Isis |language=en |volume=65 |issue=3 |pages=301–321 |doi=10.1086/351300 |issn=0021-1753 |jstor=228955|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

=== Recognition of Negus's contribution ===
Negus called up Mason and told him of her own discovery. Mason accepted Negus's priority, later declaring: "Tina Negus saw the frond before I did but no one took her seriously."<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Brasier |first1=M. |last2=Antcliffe |first2=J. |last3=Callow |first3=R. |date=2007 |title=Leicester's fossil celebrity: Charnia and the evolution of early life |journal=University of Leicester Publication |s2cid=209753590}}</ref> In 2007, Negus's role was properly recognised at the seminar at Leicester University celebrating the 50th anniversary of ''Charnia'' discovery, where she was invited alongside Mason and Ford.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Discovering Charnia |url=https://www.charnwoodforest.org/discovering-charnia/ |access-date=2025-01-27 |website=Charnwood Forest Geopark |language=en-GB}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Cassella |first=Carly |date=2023-08-05 |title=How 2 Teens Accidentally Solved Charles Darwin's Most Vexing Problem |url=https://www.sciencealert.com/how-2-teens-accidentally-solved-charles-darwins-most-vexing-problem |access-date=2025-03-05 |website=ScienceAlert |language=en-US}}</ref> The seminar ended with cutting of the "Charnia cake" by the three.<ref name="Becky" />

== Ecology of River Thames ==
In her master's degree course in zoology at the University of Reading, Negus researched on the ecology of the River Thames for her dissertation in 1964 and focussed on the diversity and abundance of freshwater mussels.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2022-11-02 |title=Mussel survey in River Thames - University of Reading |url=https://www.reading.ac.uk/news/2022/Research-News/Mussel-survey-in-River-Thames |access-date=2024-11-13 |website=www.reading.ac.uk |language=en}}</ref> She published her findings in the ''[[Journal of Animal Ecology]]'' in 1966,<ref name="Negus 1966 513–532" /> which remained unnoticed for over half a century. She reported that the major species of mussels were the duck mussel (''[[Anodonta anatina]]'') and the painter's mussel (''[[Unio pictorum]]''); ''[[Anodonta  minima|A. minima]]'' and ''[[Unio tumidus|U. tumidus]]'' were also common, and the rarest were ''[[Anodonta cygnea|A. cygnea]]''. Negus's selection of the mussels was notable in that the animals account for 90% of all living organisms recorded by weight on the Thames' riverbed.<ref name=":4" /> The importance of her research was realised and revived in 2022 when [[University of Cambridge]] scholar Isobel Ollard re-investigated the same mussel ecology at the same site.<ref name=":4" /> Since the late 1960's, it has been established that the different biological features of mussels are reliable scientific indicators of the health of the water bodies.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Seed |first=R. |date=1968 |title=Factors Influencing Shell Shape in the Mussel Mytilus Edulis |url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/journal-of-the-marine-biological-association-of-the-united-kingdom/article/abs/factors-influencing-shell-shape-in-the-mussel-mytilus-edulis/BB840D776C38871D41769B2E94358333 |journal=Journal of the Marine Biological Association of the United Kingdom |language=en |volume=48 |issue=3 |pages=561–584 |doi=10.1017/S0025315400019159 |bibcode=1968JMBUK..48..561S |issn=1469-7769|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Lopes-Lima |first1=Manuel |last2=Sousa |first2=Ronaldo |last3=Geist |first3=Juergen |last4=Aldridge |first4=David C. |last5=Araujo |first5=Rafael |last6=Bergengren |first6=Jakob |last7=Bespalaya |first7=Yulia |last8=Bódis |first8=Erika |last9=Burlakova |first9=Lyubov |last10=Van Damme |first10=Dirk |last11=Douda |first11=Karel |last12=Froufe |first12=Elsa |last13=Georgiev |first13=Dilian |last14=Gumpinger |first14=Clemens |last15=Karatayev |first15=Alexander |display-authors=8 |date=2017 |title=Conservation status of freshwater mussels in Europe: state of the art and future challenges: Conservation of European freshwater mussels |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/brv.12244 |journal=Biological Reviews |language=en |volume=92 |issue=1 |pages=572–607 |doi=10.1111/brv.12244|pmid=26727244 |url-access=subscription |hdl=10198/15259 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>

In 2023, Ollard reported her investigation in the same ''Journal of Animal Ecology.''<ref name=":5" /> Her findings revealed that the general mussel communities had declined since Negus's report by almost 95%.<ref name=":4" /><ref name=":6">{{Cite web |last=Ashworth |first=James |date=2022-11-28 |title=Mussels in the Thames have declined by 95% since the 1960s |url=https://www.nhm.ac.uk/discover/news/2022/november/mussels-thames-have-declined-by-95-since-1960s.html |access-date=2024-11-13 |website=www.nhm.ac.uk |language=en}}</ref> The duck mussels had decreased to 1.1%, and the painter’s mussel, to 3.2%; while the rare species had completely disappeared.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2022-11-28 |title=Mussel survey reveals alarming degradation of River Thames ecosystem since the 1960s {{!}} University of Cambridge |url=https://www.cam.ac.uk/research/news/mussel-survey-reveals-alarming-degradation-of-river-thames-ecosystem-since-the-1960s |access-date=2024-11-13 |website=www.cam.ac.uk |language=en}}</ref> The alarming case was not only on the number, but also on the reduced sizes of the mussels, which is a scientific method of determining the deterioration of the Thames' ecosystem. The size and growth rates had reduced by 10 to 30%.<ref name=":4" /> Ollard's supervisor and co-author David Aldridge explained the significance of the study: "While this might seem like a rather parochial little study of a single site in a single river in the UK, it actually provides an important warning signal about the world's freshwaters."<ref name=":6" /> Thames in the late 1950s and early 1960s was in its highest level of pollution; in 1957, scientists at the [[Natural History Museum of London]] considered the Thames so polluted that they declared it "biologically dead," since it would not be able to sustain any major life form.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2021-11-21 |title=The State Of The Thames 2021 |url=https://www.zsl.org/news-and-events/news/state-of-the-thames-2021 |access-date=2024-11-13 |website=www.zsl.org |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Aridi |first=Rasha |date=2021-12-21 |title=Once Deemed 'Biologically Dead,' a New Report Shows London's River Thames Recovering |url=https://www.smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/once-deemed-biologically-dead-a-new-report-shows-londons-river-thames-recovering-180979061/ |access-date=2024-11-13 |website=Smithsonian Magazine |language=en}}</ref> According to Ollard, the policies on Thames conservation had prevented the total disappearance of the mussels and the stable, albeit critically low number, is an indication that the [[river ecosystem]] is improving.<ref name=":4" />

In recognition of her pioneering work, the University of Reading commissioned the Tina Negus Prize to graduate students of biology since 2019.<ref name=":02" />
